It is true that the giving of rest from all his enemies round about does not definitely presuppose the termination of <hi type="italic">all</hi> the greater wars of David, since it is not affirmed that this rest was a definitive one; but the words cannot possibly be restricted to the two victories over the Philistines (<reference osisRef="2Sam.5.17-2Sam.5.25">2Sa 5:17-25</reference>), as Hengstenberg supposes, inasmuch as, however important the second may have been, their foes were not even permanently quieted by them, to say nothing of their being entirely subdued. Moreover, in the promise mentioned in <reference osisRef="2Sam.7.9">2Sa 7:9</reference>, God distinctly says, “I was with thee whithersoever thou wentest, and have cut off <hi type="italic">all</hi> thine enemies before thee.” These words also show that at that time David had already fought against all the enemies round about, and humbled them. Now, as all David’s principal wars are grouped together for the first time in 2 Samuel 8 and 10, there can be no doubt that the history is not arranged in a strictly chronological order. And the expression “after this” in <reference osisRef="2Sam.8.1">2Sa 8:1</reference> is by no means at variance with this, since this formula does not at all express a strictly chronological sequence. From the words of the prophet, “Go, do all that is in thy heart, for the Lord is with thee,” it is very evident that David had expressed the intention to build a splendid palatial temple. The word לך, <hi type="italic">go</hi> (equivalent to “quite right”), is omitted in the Chronicles as superfluous. Nathan sanctioned the king’s resolution “from his own feelings, and not by divine revelation” (J. H. Michaelis); but he did not “afterwards perceive that the time for carrying out this intention had not yet come,” as Thenius and Bertheau maintain; on the contrary, the Lord God revealed to the prophet that David was not to carry out his intention at all.
entries.bf50411ac0fa7334fb381aab1d68a7cac689f52d: <reference osisRef="2Sam.7.4-2Sam.7.5">2Sa 7:4-5</reference> <hi type="italic">The revelation and promise of God.</hi> - 2Sa 7:4. <hi type="italic">“That night,”</hi> i.e., the night succeeding the day on which Nathan had talked with the king concerning the building of the temple, the Lord made known His decree to the prophet, with instructions to communicate it to the king. וגו האתּה, “Shouldest thou build me a house for me to dwell in?” The question involves a negative reply, and consequently in the Chronicles we find “thou shalt not.”
entries.01b177abf8f0ef483bbe27c89ebccbc145b5adf5: <reference osisRef="2Sam.7.6-2Sam.7.7">2Sa 7:6-7</reference> <div eID="gen4322" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4323" type="x-p"/> The reason assigned for this answer: “I have not dwelt in a house from the day of the bringing up of Israel out of Egypt even to this day, but I was wandering about in a tent and in a dwelling.” <hi type="italic">“And in a dwelling”</hi> (<hi type="italic">mishcan</hi>) is to be taken as explanatory, viz., in a tent which was my dwelling. As a tent is a traveller’s dwelling, so, as long as God’s dwelling was a tent, He himself appeared as if travelling or going from place to place. “In the whole of the time that I walked among all the children of Israel, ... have I spoken a word to one of the tribes of Israel, whom I commanded to feed my people, saying, Wherefore have ye not built me a cedar house?” A “cedar house” is equivalent to a palace built of costly materials. The expression ישׂראל שׁבטי אחד (“one of the tribes of Israel”) is a striking one, as the feeding of the nation does not appear to be a duty belonging to the “tribes,” and in the Chronicles we have שׁפטי (judges) instead of שׁבטי (tribes). But if שׁפטי had been the original expression used in the text, it would be impossible to explain the origin and general acceptance of the word שׁבטי. For this very reason, therefore, we must regard שׁבטי as the original word, and understand it as referring to the <hi type="italic">tribes</hi>, which had supplied the nation with judges and leaders before the tie of David, since the feeding, i.e., the government of Israel, which was in the hands of the judges, was transferred to the tribes to which the judges belonged. This view is confirmed by <reference osisRef="Ps.78.67-Ps.78.68">Psa 78:67-68</reference>, where the election of David as prince, and of Zion as the site of the sanctuary, is described as the election of the <hi type="italic">tribe</hi> of Judah and the rejection of the tribe of Ephraim. On the other hand, the assumption of Thenius, that שׁבטי, “shepherd-staffs,” is used poetically for shepherds, cannot be established on the ground of <reference osisRef="Lev.27.32">Lev 27:32</reference> and Mic 7:14. Jehovah gave two reasons why David’s proposal to build Him a temple should not be carried out: (1) He had hitherto lived in a tent in the midst of His people; (2) He had not commanded any former prince or tribe to build a temple. This did not involve any blame, as though there had been something presumptuous in David’s proposal, or in the fact that he had thought of undertaking such a work without an express command from God, but simply showed that it was not because of any negligence on the part of the former leaders of the people that they had not thought of erecting a temple, and that even now the time for carrying out such a work as that had not yet come.
entries.fc4148d175e969b738742f2914fa06742a2446a4: <reference osisRef="2Sam.7.8-2Sam.7.16">2Sa 7:8-16</reference> <div eID="gen4323" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4324" type="x-p"/> After thus declining his proposal, the Lord made known His gracious purpose to David: “Thus saith Jehovah of hosts” (not only <hi type="italic">Jehovah</hi>, as in <reference osisRef="2Sam.7.5">2Sa 7:5</reference>, but J<hi type="italic">ehovah Sebaoth</hi>, because He manifests himself in the following revelation as the God of the universe): “I have taken thee from the pasturage (grass-plat), behind the flock, to be prince over my people Israel; and was with thee whithersoever thou wentest, and exterminated all thine enemies before thee, and so made thee, ועשׂיתי (perfect with vav consec.), a great name, ... and created a place for my people Israel, and planted them, so that they dwell in their place, and do not tremble any more (before their oppressors); and the sons of wickedness do not oppress them any further, as at the beginning, and from the day when I appointed judges over my people Israel: and I create thee rest from all thine enemies. And Jehovah proclaims to thee, that Jehovah will make thee a house.” The words ישׂ עמּי ... היּום למן are to be joined to בּראשׁונה, “as in the beginning,” i.e., in Egypt, and from the time of the judges; that is to say, during the rule of the judges, when the surrounding nations constantly oppressed and subjugated Israel. The plan usually adopted, of connecting the words with והניחתי, does not yield any suitable thought at all, as God had not given David rest from the very beginning of the times of the judges; but the period of the judges was long antecedent to the time of David, and was not a period of rest for the Israelites. Again, והניחתי does not resume what is stated in <reference osisRef="2Sam.7.9">2Sa 7:9</reference>, and is not to be rendered as a preterite in the sense of “I have procured thee rest,” but as a perfect with <hi type="italic">vav consec.</hi>, “and I procure thee rest” from what is now about to come to pass. And והגּיד is to be taken in the same way: the Lord shows thee, first of all through His promise (which follows), and then through the fact itself, the realization of His word. והניחתי refers to the future, as well as the building of David’s house, and therefore not to the rest from all his enemies, which God had already secured for David, but to that which He would still further secure for him, that is to say, to the maintenance and establishment of that rest. The commentary upon this is to be found in <reference osisRef="Ps.89.22">Psa 89:22</reference>-24. In the Chronicles (<reference osisRef="1Chr.17.10">1Ch 17:10</reference>) there is a somewhat different turn given to the last clauses: “and I bend down all thine enemies, and make it (the bending-down) known to thee (by the fact), and a house will Jehovah build for thee.” The thought is not essentially changed by this; consequently there is no ground for any emendation of the text, which is not even apparently necessary, unless, like Bertheau, we misinterpret the words, and connect והכנעתּי erroneously with the previous clause.  <reference osisRef="2Sam.7.8-2Sam.7.11">2Sa 7:8-11</reference> <div eID="gen4324" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4325" type="x-p"/> The connection between <reference osisRef="2Sam.7.5-2Sam.7.7">2Sa 7:5-7</reference> and <reference osisRef="2Sam.7.8-2Sam.7.16">2Sa 7:8-16</reference> has been correctly indicated by Thenius as follows: Thou shalt not build a house for Me; but I, who have from the very beginning glorified myself in thee and my people (<reference osisRef="2Sam.7.8-2Sam.7.11">2Sa 7:8-11</reference>), will build a house for thee; and thy son shall erect a house for me (<reference osisRef="2Sam.7.13">2Sa 7:13</reference>). This thought is not merely “a play upon words entirely in the spirit of prophecy,” but contains the deep general truth that God must first of all build a man’s house, before the man can build God’s house, and applies it especially to the kingdom of God in Israel. As long as the quiet and full possession of the land of Canaan, which had been promised by the Lord to the people of God for their inheritance, was disputed by their enemies round about, even the dwelling-place of their God could not assume any other form than that of a wanderer’s tent. The kingdom of God in Israel first acquired its rest and consolation through the efforts of David, when God had made all his foes subject to him and established his throne firmly, i.e., had assured to his descendants the possession of the kingdom for all future time. And it was this which ushered in the time for the building of a stationary house as a dwelling for the name of the Lord, i.e., for the visible manifestation of the presence of God in the midst of His people. The conquest of the citadel of Zion and the elevation of this fortress into the palace of the king, whom the Lord had given to His people, formed the commencement of the establishment of the kingdom of God. But this commencement received its first pledge of perpetuity from the divine assurance that the throne of David should be established for all future time. And this the Lord was about to accomplish: He would build David a house, and then his seed should build the house of the Lord. No definite reason is assigned why David himself was not to build the temple. We learn this first of all from David’s last words (<reference osisRef="1Chr.28.3">1Ch 28:3</reference>), in which he says to the assembled heads of the nation, “God said to me, Thou shalt not build a house for my name, because thou art a man of wars, and hast shed blood.” Compare with this the similar words of David to Solomon in <reference osisRef="1Chr.22.8">1Ch 22:8</reference>, and Solomon’s statement in his message to Hiram, that David had been prevented from building the temple in consequence of his many wars. It was probably not till afterwards that David was informed by Nathan what the true reason was. As Hengstenberg has correctly observed, the fact that David was not permitted to build the temple on account of his own personal unworthiness, did not involve any blame for what he had done; for David stood in a closer relation to the Lord than Solomon did, and the wars which he waged were wars of the Lord (<reference osisRef="1Sam.25.28">1Sa 25:28</reference>) for the maintenance and defence of the kingdom of God. But inasmuch as these wars were necessary and inevitable, they were practical proofs that David’s kingdom and government were not yet established, and therefore that the time for the building of the temple had not yet come, and the rest of peace was not yet secured. The temple, as the symbolical representation of the kingdom of God, as also to correspond to the nature of that kingdom, and shadow forth the peace of the kingdom of God. For this reason, David, the man of war, was not to build the temple; but that was to be reserved for Solomon, the man of peace, the type of the Prince of Peace (<reference osisRef="Isa.9.5">Isa 9:5</reference>).
entries.ffd3f0376f3f9ab522f084f94788fca6c5fa4455: <reference osisRef="2Sam.7.17">2Sa 7:17</reference> <hi type="italic">“According to all these words ... did Nathan speak unto David,”</hi> i.e., he related the whole to David, just as God had addressed it to him in the night. The clause in apposition, “according to all this vision,” merely introduces a more minute definition of the peculiar form of the revelation. God spoke to Nathan in a vision which he had in the night, i.e., not in a dream, but in a waking condition, and during the night; for חזּיון = חזון is constantly distinguished from חלום, a revelation in a dream.<hi type="italic">David’s prayer and thanksgiving.</hi> - 2Sa 7:18. King David came, i.e., went into the sanctuary erected upon Zion, and remained before Jehovah. ישׁב, <hi type="italic">remained, tarried</hi> (as in <reference osisRef="Gen.24.55">Gen 24:55</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gen.29.19">Gen 29:19</reference>, etc.), not <hi type="italic">“sat;”</hi> for the custom of sitting before the Lord in the sanctuary, as the posture assumed in prayer, cannot be deduced from <reference osisRef="Exod.17.12">Exo 17:12</reference>, where Moses is compelled to sit from simple exhaustion. David’s prayer consists of two parts - thanksgiving for the promise (<reference osisRef="2Sam.7.18-2Sam.7.24">2Sa 7:18-24</reference>), and supplication for its fulfilment (<reference osisRef="2Sam.7.25-2Sam.7.29">2Sa 7:25-29</reference>). The thanksgiving consists of a confession of unworthiness of all the great things that the Lord had hitherto done for him, and which He had still further increased by this glorious promise (<reference osisRef="2Sam.7.18-2Sam.7.21">2Sa 7:18-21</reference>), and praise to the Lord that all this had been done in proof of His true Deity, and to glorify His name upon His chosen people Israel.<hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="2Sam.7.18">2Sa 7:18</reference></hi>. “Who am I, O Lord Jehovah? and who my house (i.e., my family), <hi type="italic">that Thou hast brought me hitherto?</hi>” These words recall Jacob’s prayer in <reference osisRef="Gen.32.10">Gen 32:10</reference>, “I am not worthy of the least of all the mercies,” etc. David acknowledged himself to be unworthy of the great mercy which the Lord had displayed towards him, that he might give the glory to God alone (vid., <reference osisRef="Ps.8.5">Psa 8:5</reference> and <reference osisRef="Ps.144.3">Psa 144:3</reference>).
entries.25b5aa4c11103ca0fbc5fd0aeef606293f3f4a80: <reference osisRef="2Sam.7.19">2Sa 7:19</reference> <hi type="italic">“And this is still too little in Thine eyes, O Lord Jehovah, and Thou still speakest with regard to the house of Thy servant for a great while to come.”</hi> למרחוק, <hi type="italic">lit</hi>. that which points to a remote period, i.e., that of the eternal establishment of my house and throne. <hi type="italic">“And this is the law of man, O Lord Jehovah.”</hi> “The law of man” is the law which determines ore regulates the conduct of man. Hence the meaning of these words, which have been very differently interpreted, cannot, with the context immediately preceding it, be any other than the following: This - namely, the love and condescension manifested in Thy treatment of Thy servant - is the law which applies to man, or is conformed to the law which men are to observe towards men, i.e., to the law, Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself (<reference osisRef="Lev.19.18">Lev 19:18</reference>, compare Mic 6:8). With this interpretation, which is confirmed by the parallel text of the Chronicles (in <reference osisRef="2Sam.7.17">2Sa 7:17</reference>), “Thou sawest (i.e., visitedst me, or didst deal with me) according to the manner of man,” that words are expressive of praise of the condescending grace of the Lord. “When God the Lord, in His treatment of poor mortals, follows the rule which He has laid down for the conduct of men one towards another, when He shows himself kind and affectionate, this must fill with adoring amazement those who know themselves and God” (<hi type="italic">Hengstenberg</hi>). Luther is wrong in the rendering which he has adopted: “This is the manner of a man, who is God the Lord;” for “Lord Jehovah” is not an explanatory apposition to “man,” but an address to God, as in the preceding and following clause.
entries.adff9fa38ba6b819b22068a52395112c083661b1: <reference osisRef="2Sam.7.20">2Sa 7:20</reference> <hi type="italic">“And what more shall David speak to Thee? Thou knowest Thy servant, Lord Jehovah.”</hi> Instead of expressing his gratitude still further in many words, David appeals to the omniscience of God, before whom his thankful heart lies open, just as in <reference osisRef="Ps.40.10">Psa 40:10</reference> (compare also <reference osisRef="Ps.17.3">Psa 17:3</reference>).
entries.2c6a7ae7019efaa70ac8581cdd8038dd477865cd: <reference osisRef="2Sam.7.21-2Sam.7.22">2Sa 7:21-22</reference> <hi type="italic">“For Thy word’s sake, and according to Thy heart </hi>(and therefore not because I am worthy of such grace),<hi type="italic">has Thou done all this greatness, to make it known to Thy servant.”</hi> The word, for the sake of which God had done such great things for David, must be some former promise on the part of God. Hengstenberg supposes it to refer to the word of the Lord to Samuel, “Rise up and anoint him” (<reference osisRef="1Sam.16.12">1Sa 16:12</reference>), which is apparently favoured indeed by the parallel in the corresponding text of <reference osisRef="1Chr.17.19">1Ch 17:19</reference>, “for Thy servant’s sake,” i.e., because Thou hast chosen Thy servant. But even this variation must contain some special allusion which does not exclude a <hi type="italic">general</hi> interpretation of the expression “for Thy word’s sake,” viz., an allusion to the earlier promises of God, or the Messianic prophecies generally, particularly the one concerning Judah in Jacob’s blessing (<reference osisRef="Gen.49.10">Gen 49:10</reference>), and the one relating to the ruler out of Jacob in Balaam’s sayings (Num 24:17.), which contain the germs of the promise of the everlasting continuance of David’s government. For the fact that David recognised the connection between the promise of God communicated to him by Nathan and Jacob’s prophecy in <reference osisRef="Gen.49.10">Gen 49:10</reference>, is evident from <reference osisRef="1Chr.28.4">1Ch 28:4</reference>, where he refers to his election as king as being the consequence of the election of Judah as ruler. “According to Thine own heart” is equivalent to “according to Thy love and grace; for God is gracious, merciful, and of great kindness and truth” (<reference osisRef="Exod.34.6">Exo 34:6</reference>, compare <reference osisRef="Ps.103.8">Psa 103:8</reference>). גּדוּלה does not mean great things, but greatness. <div eID="gen4328" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4329" type="x-p"/> The praise of God commences in <reference osisRef="2Sam.7.22">2Sa 7:22</reference> : <hi type="italic">“wherefore Thou art great, Jehovah God; and there is not (one) like Thee, and no God beside Thee, according to all that we have heard with our ears.”</hi> By the word “wherefore,” i.e., because Thou hast done this, the praise of the singleness of God is set forth as the result of David’s own experience. God is great when He manifests the greatness of His grace to men, and brings them to acknowledge it. And in these great deeds He proves the incomparable nature of His Deity, or that He alone is the true God. (For the fact itself, compare <reference osisRef="Exod.15.11">Exo 15:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.3.24">Deu 3:24</reference>; Deu 4:35.)
entries.a46e44b266e94d5c2d216df0673282f2a661d488: <reference osisRef="2Sam.7.23">2Sa 7:23</reference> <hi type="italic">“And where is </hi>(any)<hi type="italic">like Thy people, like Israel, a nation upon earth, which God went to redeem as a people for himself, that He might make Him a name, and do great things for you, and terrible things for Thy land before Thy people, which Thou hast redeemed for Thee out of Egypt, </hi>(out of the)<hi type="italic">nations and their gods?”</hi> מי does not really mean <hi type="italic">where</hi>, but <hi type="italic">who</hi>, and is to be connected with the words immediately following, viz., אחד גּוי (one nation); but the only way in which the words can be rendered into good English (<hi type="italic">German</hi> in the original: Tr.) is, “where is there any people,” etc. The relative אשׁר does not belong to הלכוּ, “which Elohim went to redeem.” The construing of <hi type="italic">Elohim</hi> with a plural arises from the fact, that in this clause it not only refers to the true God, but also includes the idea of the gods of other nations. The idea, therefore, is not, “Is there any nation upon earth to which the only true God went?” but, “Is there any nation to which the deity worshipped by it went, as the true God went to Israel to redeem it for His own people?” The rendering given in the Septuagint to הלכוּ, viz., ὠδήγησεν, merely arose from a misapprehension of the true sense of the words; and the emendation הוליך, which some propose in consequence, would only distort the sense. The stress laid upon the incomparable character of the things which God had done for Israel, is merely introduced to praise and celebrate the God who did this as the only true God. (For the thought itself, compare the original passage in <reference osisRef="Deut.4.7">Deu 4:7</reference>, Deu 4:34.) In the clause לכם ולעשׂות, “and to do for you,” David addresses the people of Israel with oratorical vivacity. Instead of saying “to do great things to (for) Israel,” he says “to do great things to (for <hi type="italic">you</hi>.” <hi type="italic">For you </hi>forms an antithesis to <hi type="italic">him</hi>, “to make Him a name, and to do great things for you (Israel).” The suggestion made by some, that לכם is to be taken as a <hi type="italic">dativ. comm.</hi>, and referred to <hi type="italic">Elohim</hi>, no more needs a serious refutation than the alteration into להם. There have been different opinions, however, as to the object referred to in the suffix attached to לארצך, and it is difficult to decide between them; for whilst the fact that לארצך נראות (terrible things to Thy land) is governed by לעשׂות (to do) favours the allusion to Israel, and the sudden transition from the plural to the singular might be accounted for from the deep emotion of the person speaking, the words which follow (“before Thy people”) rather favour the allusion to God, as it does not seem natural to take the suffix in two different senses in the two objects which follow so closely the one upon the other, viz., <hi type="italic">“for Thy land,”</hi> and <hi type="italic">“before Thy people;”</hi> whilst the way is prepared for a transition from speaking of God to speaking to God by the word לכם (to you). The words of <reference osisRef="Deut.10.21">Deu 10:21</reference> floated before the mind of David at the time, although he has given them a different turn. (On the “terrible things,” see the commentary on <reference osisRef="Deut.10.21">Deu 10:21</reference> and Exo 15:11.) The connection of נראות (terrible things) with לארצך (to Thy land) shows that David had in mind, when speaking of the acts of divine omnipotence which had inspired fear and dread of the majesty of God, not only the miracles of God in Egypt, but also the marvellous extermination of the Canaanites, whereby Israel had been established in the possession of the promised land, and the people of God placed in a condition to found a kingdom. These acts were performed <hi type="italic">before</hi> Israel, before the nation, whom the Lord redeemed to himself out of Egypt. This view is confirmed by the last words, “nations and their gods,” which are in apposition to “from Egypt,” so that the preposition מן should be repeated before גּוים (nations). The suffix to ואלהיו (literally “and <hi type="italic">its</hi> gods”) is to be regarded as distributive: “the gods of each of these heathen nations.” In the Chronicles (<reference osisRef="1Chr.17.21">1Ch 17:21</reference>) the expression is simplified, and explained more clearly by the omission of “to Thy land,” and the insertion of לגרשׁ, “to drive out nations from before Thy people.” It has been erroneously inferred from this, that the text of our book is corrupt, and ought to be emended, or at any rate interpreted according to the Chronicles. But whilst לארצך is certainly not to be altered into לגרשׁ, it is just as wrong to do as <hi type="italic">Hengstenberg</hi> proposes, - namely, to take the thought expressed in לגרשׁ from the preceding לעשׂות by assuming a <hi type="italic">zeugma</hi>; for עשׂה, to do or make, has nothing in common with driving or clearing away.
entries.ea2561f62e98d121cc316779fabfdf0de098f4d5: <reference osisRef="2Sam.7.24-2Sam.7.26">2Sa 7:24-26</reference> <hi type="italic">“And Thou hast established to thyself Thy people Israel to be a people unto Thee for ever: and Thou, Jehovah, hast become a God to them.”</hi> The first clause does not refer merely to the liberation of Israel out of Egypt, or to the conquest of Canaan alone, but to all that the Lord had done for the establishment of Israel as the people of His possession, from the time of Moses till His promise of the eternal continuance of the throne of David. Jehovah had thereby become God to the nation of Israel, i.e., had thereby attested and proved himself to be its God. <div eID="gen4329" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4330" type="x-p"/> To this praise of the acts of the Lord there is attached in 2Sa 7:25. the prayer for the fulfilment of His glorious promise. Would Jehovah set up (i.e., carry out) the word which He had spoken to His servant that His name might be great, i.e., be glorified, through its being said, “The Lord of Sabaoth is God over Israel,” and “the house of Thy servant will be firm before Thee.” The prayer is expressed in the form of confident assurance.
entries.a920eb0f2494710231b277b3c53e53798d0c4f70: <reference osisRef="2Sam.7.27">2Sa 7:27</reference> <div eID="gen4330" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4331" type="x-p"/> David felt himself encouraged to offer this prayer through the revelation which he had received. Because God had promised to build him a house, “therefore Thy servant hath found in his heart to pray this prayer,” i.e., hath found joy in doing so.
entries.761a67faae16f007ab03cf0c814025d4005e15a0: <reference osisRef="2Sam.7.28-2Sam.7.29">2Sa 7:28-29</reference> <div eID="gen4331" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4332" type="x-p"/> David then briefly sums up the two parts of his prayer of thanksgiving in the two clauses commencing with ועתּה, “and now.” - In <reference osisRef="2Sam.7.28">2Sa 7:28</reference> he sums up the contents of <reference osisRef="2Sam.7.18-2Sam.7.24">2Sa 7:18-24</reference> by celebrating the greatness of the Lord and His promise; and in <reference osisRef="2Sam.7.29">2Sa 7:29</reference> the substance of the prayer in <reference osisRef="2Sam.7.25">2Sa 7:25</reference>-27. וּברך הואל, may it please Thee to bless (הואיל; see at <reference osisRef="Deut.1.5">Deu 1:5</reference>). “And from (out of) Thy blessing may the house of Thy servant be blessed for ever.” David’s Wars, Victories, and Ministers of State - 2 Samuel 8 <div eID="gen4332" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4333" type="x-p"/> To the promise of the establishment of this throne there is appended a general enumeration of the wars by which David secured the supremacy of Israel over all his enemies round about. In this survey all the nations are included with which war had ever been waged by David, and which he had conquered and rendered tributary: the Philistines and Moabites, the Syrians of Zobah and Damascus, Toi of Hamath, the Ammonites, Amalekites, and Edomites. It is very evident from this, that the chapter before us not only treats of the wars which David carried on after receiving the divine promise mentioned in 2 Samuel 7, but of all the wars of his entire reign. The only one of which we have afterwards a fuller account is the war with the Ammonites and their allies the Syrians (2 Samuel 10 and 11), and this is given on account of its connection with David’s adultery. In the survey before us, the war with the Ammonites is only mentioned quite cursorily in <reference osisRef="2Sam.8.12">2Sa 8:12</reference>, in the account of the booty taken from the different nations, which David dedicated to the Lord. With regard to the other wars, so far as the principal purpose was concerned-namely, to record the history of the kingdom of God-it was quite sufficient to give a general statement of the fact that these nations were smitten by David and subjected to his sceptre. But if this chapter contains a survey of all the wars of David with the nations that were hostile to Israel, there can be no doubt that the arrangement of the several events is not strictly regulated by their chronological order, but that homogeneous events are grouped together according to a material point of view. There is a parallel to this chapter in 1 Chron 18.  <chapter eID="2Sam.7"/> <div eID="gen4333" type="x-p"/>

                  <ns0:p n="2">2 That the king said unto Nathan the prophet, See now, I dwell in an house of Cedar, but the ark of God dwelleth within curtains <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> In a Tent or Tabernacle, <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 6. composed of several Curtains, <ns0:hi>Exod.</ns0:hi> 26. 1, &c.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="3">3 And Nathan said to the king, Go, do all that <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> in thine heart <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">Pursue thy intentions, and Build an House for the Ark. And therefore <ns0:hi>Nathan</ns0:hi> meets with this rebuke, that he is forced to acknowledge his error, and recant it. For the Holy Prophets did not speak all things by Prophetical Inspiration, but some things by an human spirit, and prudent conjecture; and therefore they were ig<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />norant and mistaken in some matters, as 1 <ns0:hi>Sam.</ns0:hi> 16. 6. 2 <ns0:hi>King.</ns0:hi> 4. 27.</ns0:note>: for the LORD <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> with thee.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="4">4 ¶ And it came to pass that night <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">Because <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi>'s mistake was Fious, and from an honest mind, God would not suffer him to lie long in his mistake, nor to disquiet his mind, or run himself into inconveni<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />encies, in order to the Work, before he gave a stop to it.</ns0:note>, that the word of the LORD came unto Nathan <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">That the same Person who had confirmed <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi> in his mistake, might now rectify it.</ns0:note>, say<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing,</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="5">5 Go and tell <ns0:note n="‡" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> to my servant, to David.</ns0:note> my servant David, Thus saith the LORD, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">See 1 Kin. 5. 3. 1 Chron. 22. 8. and 28. 3.</ns0:note> Shalt thou build <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> Thou shalt not. Or, <ns0:hi>wiltst thou build,</ns0:hi> &c? Dost thou purpose it?</ns0:note> me an house for me to dwell in?</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="6">6 Whereas I have not dwelt in <ns0:hi>any</ns0:hi> house, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">1 King. 8. 16</ns0:note> since the time that I brought up the children of Israel out of Egypt, even to this day, but have walked in a tent, and in a tabernacle <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">These two seem thus to be distinguished, the one may note the Curtains and Hangings within, the other the Frame of Boards, and Coverings upon it.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="7">7 In all <ns0:hi>the places</ns0:hi> wherein I have walked with all the children of Israel, spake I a word <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">Did I ever give any command about it, without which neither they did, nor thou shouldst attempt it?</ns0:note> with <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">1 Chr. 17. 6. any of the Judges.</ns0:note> any of the tribes <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">In 1 <ns0:hi>Chron.</ns0:hi> 17. 6. it is <ns0:hi>of the Iudges,</ns0:hi> and to them, not to the Tribes, the following words agree, <ns0:hi>whom I commanded to feed my people</ns0:hi> Israel.                      <ns0:pb facs="tcp:107763:252" />8 Now therefore, so shalt thou say unto my ser<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vant David <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">Lest <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi> should be too much discouraged, or judge himself neglected and forsaken of God, as one thought un<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />worthy of so great an honour, God here gives him the honou<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rable title of <ns0:hi>his Servant,</ns0:hi> thereby signifying that he accepted of his service, and of his good intentions, which also was expressed at this time, as it may seem from 1 <ns0:hi>King.</ns0:hi> 8. 18. though not in this place.</ns0:note>: Thus saith the LORD of hosts, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">1 Sam. 16. 11, 12. Psal. 78. 71.</ns0:note> I took thee from the sheep-coat, <ns0:note n="‡" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> from after.</ns0:note> from follow<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing the sheep, to be ruler over my people, over Israel <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">I advanced thee, and I do not repent of it.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="9">9 And I was with thee whithersoever thou wentest, and have cut off all thine enemies <ns0:note n="‡" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> from thy face.</ns0:note> out of thy sight, and have made thee a great name, like unto the name of the great <ns0:hi>men</ns0:hi> that are in the earth.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="10">10 (Moreover, I will appoint a place <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> I will make room for them, whereas hitherto they have been much straitned and distressed by their Enemies. Or, <ns0:hi>I will establish</ns0:hi> (for so that Verb sometimes signifies) <ns0:hi>a place</ns0:hi> for them, <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> I will establish them in their Place or Land. Some learned Men render the Verse thus, and the <ns0:hi>Hebrew</ns0:hi> words will bear it: <ns0:hi>And I have appointed</ns0:hi> (or, <ns0:hi>assigned,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>given) a place for my people Israel</ns0:hi> (to wit, the Land of <ns0:hi>Ca<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />naan) and have planted them</ns0:hi> in it, <ns0:hi>that they may dwell in their own place, and be no more driven to and fro:</ns0:hi> or rather, <ns0:hi>and they shall dwell in their own place,</ns0:hi> &c. <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> As I did long ago appoint it to them, and afterwards planted them, or put them into actual possession, so now they shall con<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tinue or dwell in it, in spight of all their Enemies.</ns0:note> for my people Israel <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">Among the favours which God had vouchsafed, and would vouch<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />safe to <ns0:hi>David,</ns0:hi> he reckons his Blessings to the people of <ns0:hi>Is<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rael,</ns0:hi> because they were great Blessings to <ns0:hi>David;</ns0:hi> partly, because the strength and happiness of a King consists in great part in the multitude and happiness of his People; and part<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ly, because <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi> was a Man of a pious and publick spirit, and therefore no less affected with <ns0:hi>Israel</ns0:hi>'s felicity than with his own.</ns0:note>, and will plant them, that they may dwell in a place of their own <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> In their own Land, not in strange Lands, nor mixed with other people.</ns0:note>, and move no more: neither shall the children of wickedness afflict them any more, as before-time <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">Either, First, As in the Land of <ns0:hi>Egypt:</ns0:hi> and so he goes downward to the Judges.                   <ns0:p n="11">11 And as since the time that I commanded judges <ns0:hi>to be</ns0:hi> over my people Israel <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">Nor as they did under the Judges, neither so oft, nor so long. But all this is to be understood with a condition, ex<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cept they should notoriously forsake God, or rebel against him: which being so oft declared by God in other places, it was needless to mention it here. Or, this may relate to the later Ages of the World, when the people of <ns0:hi>Israel</ns0:hi> shall be converted to Christ, and recalled out of Captivity, and planted in their own place; when they shall enjoy a far greater degree of Tranquility than ever they did before. And this agrees best with the Future Tense, <ns0:hi>I will appoint——and will plant them,</ns0:hi> &c. otherwise the work was al<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ready done, God had already appointed this Land for them, and actually planted them in it.</ns0:note>, and <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Or,</ns0:hi> I will cause. So <ns0:hi>Gr.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note> have caused thee to rest from all thine enemies <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> And until this time in which I have given thee rest. But these words though ac<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cording to our Translation they be inclosed in the same Pa<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />renthesis with the foregoing clauses, may seem to be better put without it, and to be taken by themselves. For the foregoing words in this Verse, and in <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 10. do all concern the people of <ns0:hi>Israel;</ns0:hi> but these words seem to concern <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi> alone, to whom the Speech returns after a short digression concerning the people of <ns0:hi>Israel.</ns0:hi> And they may be rendred either thus, <ns0:hi>And I have caused thee to rest,</ns0:hi> &c. or, <ns0:hi>And I will cause thee to rest,</ns0:hi> &c. to wit, more fully and perfectly than yet thou dost.</ns0:note>.) Also the LORD telleth thee, That he will make thee an house <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">For thy good intentions to make him an house, <ns0:hi>he will make thee an house,</ns0:hi> to wit, <ns0:hi>a sure house,</ns0:hi> as is expressed, 1 <ns0:hi>King.</ns0:hi> 11. 38. <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> he will encrease and uphold thy Posterity, and continue the Kingdom in thy Family.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="12">12 ¶ And <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">1 King. 8. 20.</ns0:note> when thy days be fulfilled <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">When the time of thy life shall expire.                      </ns0:note> before thee <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">Thine Eyes in some sort beholding it: for he lived to see his Wise and Godly Son <ns0:hi>Solomon</ns0:hi> actually placed in the Throne, with great reputation and general applause, 1 <ns0:hi>King.</ns0:hi> 1. 39, 40. which was in it self a good presage of the continuance of the Kingdom in his Family; and being considered toge<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther with the infallible certainty of Gods promise to him and his for ever, of the accomplishment whereof, this was an earnest, gave him good assurance thereof; especially con<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sidering that he had his eyes and thoughts upon the Messiah, <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 110. 1, &c. whose <ns0:hi>day he saw</ns0:hi> by Faith, as <ns0:hi>Abraham</ns0:hi> did, <ns0:hi>Ioh.</ns0:hi> 8. 56. and whom he <ns0:hi>knew that God would raise out of the fruit of his Loins to sit on his Throne,</ns0:hi> as is affirmed, <ns0:hi>Act.</ns0:hi> 2. 30. and that for ever: and so the Eternity of his Kingdom is rightly said to be before him.                   <ns0:p n="18">
                     <ns0:pb facs="tcp:107763:252" />18 ¶ Then went king David in, and sat <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">This word may note either, first, his Bodily gesture: for there is no certain gesture to which Prayer is limited; and we have examples of Saints Praying in that Posture, <ns0:hi>Exod.</ns0:hi> 17. 12. 1 <ns0:hi>King.</ns0:hi> 19. 4. or, he might sit for a season whilst he was Meditating upon these things, and then alter his Po<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sture (though it be not here expressed) and betake himself to Prayer.                   <ns0:p n="19">19 And this <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">To wit, which thou hast already done for me, as he now said, <ns0:hi>That thou hast brought me hitherto,</ns0:hi> i. e. to that pitch of Honour, and Peace, and Prosperity, in which through thy favour I now stand.</ns0:note> was yet a small thing in thy sight, O LORD God <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">Though it was more than I de<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />served or could expect, yet thou didst not think it enough for thee to give to me.</ns0:note>: but thou hast spoken also of thy servants house for a great while to come <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">For many future Ages, and in<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />deed to all Eternity.</ns0:note>, and <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> this the <ns0:note n="‡" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> law.</ns0:note> manner of man, O LORD God <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">Do men use to deal so freely and kindly with their inferiors, as thou hast done with me?
